analysis.one_liner: Shut down abusive online payday lending with registration, state rate caps, and bank-account protections.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 17 cosponsors in February 2018, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the same day and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targeted online payday and other small-dollar lenders. It would have required lenders making loans up to $5,000 to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, forced internet and bank-issued small-dollar loans to obey the interest-rate and fee caps of the borrower's home state, restricted how lenders tap borrowers' bank accounts, banned overdraft fees on prepaid cards, and largely shut out companies that collect and resell payday-loan applicants' personal financial information [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income borrowers who use payday and other small-dollar loans, especially those taking loans online or through prepaid cards. The bill would have made it harder for lenders to pull payments directly out of borrowers' bank accounts through remotely created checks and one-time electronic transfers without meaningful consent, required internet lenders to follow state interest-rate limits, required lenders to register with the consumer bureau, and banned overdraft fees on prepaid accounts [S3]. A required study on credit access in Indian country was meant to inform future policy on tribal lending [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Required any person issuing small-dollar consumer credit (loans up to $5,000, or a higher amount set by rule) to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before lending, with a broad definition that also covered brokers and application gatherers.

Required online, phone, mail, and other remote small-dollar loans — and loans made by national banks — to comply with the interest-rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, closing a channel lenders used to charge rates the borrower's own state forbids.

Limited remotely created checks — checks a lender can draw on a borrower's account without a signed check — to people the consumer has designated in writing with their bank, with a right to revoke the designation at any time, and barred payment orders issued in response to a consumer exercising consumer-protection rights.
Banned overdraft fees on prepaid accounts and allowed the bureau to bar additional prepaid fees by rule, directly affecting low-income consumers who load payday loan proceeds onto prepaid cards.

Prohibited companies from collecting and distributing borrowers' sensitive financial information (Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, access codes) for small-dollar loans unless they are the ones directly making the loan, and required disclosure of who they are and how to reach them.

Expanded existing protections against unauthorized electronic fund transfers — extending them beyond preauthorized transfers to one-time transfers generally — so consumers gain the existing statutory remedies when a lender takes money from their account.

analysis.who_pays: Online and storefront payday and installment lenders would have lost the ability to charge rates above a borrower's home-state caps, to pull payments directly from borrowers' bank accounts, and to operate without federal registration. Lead-generation firms — companies that collect applicants' sensitive financial data and sell it to lenders — would have lost most of that business for small-dollar loans. Prepaid card programs that charge overdraft fees, and banks that partner with payday lenders to originate loans, would have lost those revenue streams.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online payday lenders and lead-generation brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill's state-rate-cap and registration requirements could shrink the supply of short-term credit for borrowers with poor credit who cannot qualify for bank loans, pushing some toward unlicensed or informal lenders; the bill itself ordered a study of how small-dollar credit affects economic opportunity for members of Indian tribes, an implicit acknowledgment that restricting these loans has consequences for communities that rely on them.

Applying state interest-rate caps to loans made by national banks intrudes on an area national banks have long argued is governed by federal law, a change banks and their defenders would contest as an overreach that could discourage banks from serving higher-risk borrowers.

The bill leaned heavily on Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rulemaking to work, leaving key definitions — what counts as covered loans, prepaid accounts, and payment orders — to a regulator whose rules could later be changed or undone by a different administration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted at people with few defenses: lenders would no longer be able to yank money from bank accounts without a signed check or a clear authorization, internet lenders would face the same rate limits as lenders serving borrowers in person, and prepaid overdraft fees would disappear. The honest cost is that some borrowers who currently use payday loans would lose access to that credit, and it is unclear what replaces it — the bill ordered a study of tribal lending rather than answering that question directly. On balance, the bill's protections address documented harms of online payday lending without banning small loans outright.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley and 16 colleagues introduced the SAFE Lending Act in the Senate on February 13, 2018.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote through the end of the 115th Congress.
The committee's counterpart consideration never happened in either chamber; the House never took up the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online payday lenders, lead-generation firms, and prepaid-card overdraft-fee programs keep operating under pre-2018 rules; borrowers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online payday lenders and lead brokers

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 13, 2018 and led 16 Senate cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in February 2018 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Senate Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Banking Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill required federal registration, applied borrowers' home-state interest-rate and fee caps to internet and bank-issued loans, and restricted lenders' ability to draw payments directly from bank accounts. The industry's profits depend on charging rates and fees those changes would limit, so its interest ran against borrowers'.

The bill barred collecting and distributing borrowers' Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and access codes for small-dollar loans unless the collector is the direct lender, and required public identification of facilitators. These firms make money routing sensitive borrower data to lenders, at borrowers' privacy risk.
The bill banned overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, a fee charged disproportionately to low-income users who load loan proceeds onto cards. Issuers would lose that revenue.

industries.industry: National banks partnering with payday lenders
industries.note: The bill subjected loans conducted by national banks to the borrower's home-state rate caps, limiting the bank-partner structure some high-rate lenders use to export their home state's laws.

Home-state rate caps would apply to remote small-dollar loans, reaching tribal online lenders that rely on their tribal home states' laws; the bill ordered a GAO study on capital availability on reservations and required consultation with tribes before further policy.
